L1075@P14: The Southern Ocean is important for the transfer of heat from the
L1076@P14: atmosphere to the global ocean, including heat from anthropogenic
L1077@P14: warming (Frölicher et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2018). The Southern
L1078@P14: Ocean accounted for ~75% of the global ocean uptake of excess
L1079@P14: heat during 1870–1995 (Figure SM3.2; Frölicher et al., 2015), of
L1080@P14: which ~43% resided in the Southern Ocean with the remainder
L1081@P14: redistributed to lower latitudes. Over 1970–2017, observations show
L1082@P14: that the upper 2000 m of the ocean south of 30ºS was responsible
L1083@P14: for 35–43% of the increase in global ocean heat content (Table 3.1).
L1084@P14: Both models and observations show that, relative to its size (Table
L1085@P14: SM3.1), the Southern Ocean is disproportionately important in the
L1086@P14: increase in global upper ocean heat content (high confidence).
L1087@P14: Multi-decadal warming of the Southern Ocean has been attributed
L1088@P14: to anthropogenic factors, especially the role of greenhouse gases but
L1089@P14: also ozone depletion (Armour et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2018; Swart
L1090@P14: et al., 2018; Irving et al., 2019) (medium confidence).
L1091@P14: Surface warming during 1982–2016 was strongest along the northern
L1092@P14: flank of the ACC, contrasting with cooling further south (Figure 3.3).
L1093@P14: Interior warming was strongest in the upper 2000  m, peaking
L1094@P14: around 40ºS–50ºS (Armour et al., 2016) (SM3.2.1; Figures SM3.2 and
L1095@P14: SM3.3). There is high confidence that this pattern of change is driven
L1096@P14: by upper-ocean overturning circulation and mixing (Cross-Chapter
L1097@P14: Box 7 in Chapter 3), whereby heat uptake at the surface by newly
L1098@P14: upwelled waters is transmitted to the ocean interior in intermediate
L1099@P14: depth layers (Armour et al., 2016). Whilst temperature trends in the
L1100@P14: ACC itself are driven predominantly by air-sea flux changes (Swart
L1101@P14: et al., 2018), the warming on its northern side appears strongly
L1102@P14: influenced by wind-forced changes in the thickness and depth of
L1103@P14: the mode water layer (Desbruyeres et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2018)
L1104@P14: (medium confidence). Below the surface south of the ACC, warming
L1105@P14: extends close to Antarctica, intruding onto the continental shelf in
L1106@P14: the Amundsen-Bellingshausen Sea where temperature increases
L1107@P14: of  0.1ºC–0.3ºC per decade have been observed over 1983–2012
L1108@P14: (Schmidtko et al., 2014) (Section 3.3.1.5). This latter warming may be
L1109@P14: driven by changes in wind forcing (Spence et al., 2014), and exhibits
L1110@P14: significant decadal variability (Jenkins et al., 2018).
L1111@P14: After around 2005, improved upper ocean heat content estimates
L1112@P14: became available via Argo profiling floats (Section 1.8.1; Section 5.2).
L1113@P14: For 2005–2017, multiple datasets show that the heat gained by the
L1114@P14: Southern Ocean south of 30ºS was 45–62% of the global ocean heat
L1115@P14: gain (Table  3.1) (equivalent figures for other indicative Southern
L1116@P14: Ocean extents are in Table SM3.2). This accords with Roemmich et al.
L1117@P14: (2015), who found that during 2006–2013 the ocean south of 20ºS
L1118@P14: accounted for 67–98% of total heat gain in the upper 2000 m of the
L1119@P14: global ocean. (The smaller proportion for 2005–2017 c.f. 2006–2013
L1120@P14: is due to comparatively greater warming in the earlier part of the
L1121@P14: common period). The recent Southern Ocean heat gain is thus larger
L1122@P14: than its long-term trend over either the preceding several decades
L1123@P14: (1970–2004, 30–51%, Table SM3.3) or the full period 1970–2017
L1124@P14: (35–43%; Table  3.1 and above). There is high confidence that the
L1125@P14: Southern Ocean has increased its role in global ocean heat content in
L1126@P14: recent years compared with the past several decades. Attribution of
L1127@P14: this increased role is currently lacking.

L1355@P16: 3.2.1.3 Ocean Circulation
L1356@P16: The major elements of Southern Ocean circulation are assessed
L1357@P16: in Cross-Chapter Box 7  in Chapter  3; Arctic Ocean circulation is
L1358@P16: considered here. Arctic processes, such as discharge of freshwater
L1359@P16: from the Greenland Ice Sheet, have the potential to impact
L1360@P16: on the formation of the headwaters of the Atlantic Meridional
L1361@P16: Overturning Circulation (Section  6.7.1), and can impact on the
L1362@P16: structure and function of the marine ecosystem with implications for
L1363@P16: commercially-harvested species (Sections 3.2.3, 3.2.4).
L1364@P16: Satellite data indicate a  general strengthening of the surface
L1365@P16: geostrophic currents in the Arctic basin (Armitage et al., 2017).
L1366@P16: Between 2003 and 2014, the strength of some currents in the Beaufort
L1367@P16: Gyre approximately doubled (Armitage et al., 2017). Over 2001–2014,
L1368@P16: annual Bering Strait volume transport from the Pacific to the Arctic
L1369@P16: Ocean increased from 0.7 × 106 m3s–1 to 1.2 × 106 m3s–1 (Woodgate
L1370@P16: et al., 2015). Mesoscale eddies are characterised by horizontal scales
L1371@P16: of ~10 km in the Arctic, and are important components of the ocean
L1372@P16: system. Increased wind power input to the Arctic Ocean system can
L1373@P16: in principle be compensated by the production of eddy kinetic energy;
L1374@P16: analysis of observations in the Beaufort Gyre region suggest this is
L1375@P16: about as likely as not (Meneghello et al., 2017). Data of sufficiently
L1376@P16: high resolution is limited in the boundary regions of the Arctic Ocean,
L1377@P16: precluding estimates of eddy variability on a basin-wide scale. In the
L1378@P16: central basin regions, a statistically significant higher concentration of
L1379@P16: eddies was sampled in the Canadian Basin compared to the Eurasian
L1380@P16: Basin between 2003 and 2014; further, a  medium correspondence
L1381@P16: was found between eddy activity in the Beaufort Gyre region and
L1382@P16: intensified gyre flow (Zhao et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2016).
L1383@P16: In contrast to the Southern Ocean (Cross-Chapter Box 7 in Chapter 3),
L1384@P16: there is comparatively little knowledge on changing Arctic frontal
L1385@P16: positions and current cores since AR5. An exception is that the
L1386@P16: Beaufort Gyre expanded to the northwest between 2003 and 2014,

L1388@P16: alterations in wind forcing, resulting in increased proximity to the

L1394@P17: Authors: Michael P. Meredith (UK), Robert Hallberg (US), Alessandro Tagliabue (UK), Andrew Meijers (UK/Australia), Jamie Oliver (UK),

L1396@P17: Horizontal Circulation and Movement of Fronts
L1397@P17: The Southern Ocean is disproportionately important in global climate and ecological systems, being the major connection linking the
L1398@P17: Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans in the global circulation. The horizontal circulation in the circumpolar Southern Ocean is comprised
L1399@P17: of an eastward-flowing mean current concentrated in a series of sinuous, braided jets exhibiting strong meandering variability and
L1400@P17: shedding small-scale transient eddies (Figure CB7.1). The mean flow circumnavigates Antarctica as the world’s largest ocean current,
L1401@P17: the Antarctic Circumpolar Current (ACC), transporting approximately 173.3 ± 10.7 × 106 m3 s–1 (Donohue et al., 2016) of water
L1402@P17: eastward in a geostrophic balance set up by the contrasting properties of waters around Antarctica and those inside the subtropical
L1403@P17: gyres to the north of ACC. This contrast is maintained by a combination of strong westerly winds and ocean heat loss south of the ACC.
L1404@P17: Trends in the atmospheric forcing of the Southern Ocean are dominated by a strengthening of westerly winds in recent decades (Swart
L1405@P17: et al., 2015a), but there is no evidence that this enhanced wind stress has significantly altered the ACC transport. While the annual
L1406@P17: mean value of transport is stable in the instrumental period (Chidichimo et al., 2014; Koenig et al., 2014; Donohue et al., 2016) it is
L1407@P17: difficult to resolve changes in barotropic transport; overall there is medium confidence that ACC transport is only weakly sensitive
L1408@P17: to changes in winds. This is consistent with longer-term analyses that find only minimal changes in ACC transport since the last
L1409@P17: glaciation (McCave et al., 2013). Theoretical predictions and high-resolution ocean modelling suggest that the weak sensitivity of the
L1410@P17: ACC to changes in wind stress is a consequence of eddy saturation (Munday et al., 2013), whereby the time-mean state of the ocean
L1411@P17: remains close to a marginal condition for eddy instability and hence additional energy input from stronger winds cascades rapidly
L1412@P17: into the smaller-scale eddy field. Satellite measurements of eddy kinetic energy over the last two decades are consistent with this,
L1413@P17: showing a statistically significant upward trend in eddy energy in the Pacific and Indian Ocean sectors of the Southern Ocean (Hogg
L1414@P17: et al., 2015) (medium confidence). This is supported by eddy-resolving models, which also show a marked regional variability (Patara
L1415@P17: et al., 2016), and there is evidence that local hotspots in eddy energy, especially downstream of major topographic features including
L1416@P17: the Drake Passage, Kerguelen Plateau, Campbell Plateau and the East Pacific Rise, may dominate the regional fields (Thompson and
L1417@P17: Naveira Garabato, 2014).
L1418@P17: Working Group I (WGI) of the IPCC’s 5th Assessment Report (AR5) assessed that there was medium confidence that the mean position
L1419@P17: of the ACC had moved southwards in response to a contraction of the Southern Ocean circumpolar winds. Such movements can in
L1420@P17: principle have profound effects on marine ecosystems via, e.g., changing habitat ranges for different species (e.g., Cristofari et al., 2018;
L1421@P17: Meijers et al., 2019) (Section 3.2.3.2). Since AR5, however, substantial contrary evidence has emerged. While winds have strengthened
L1422@P17: over the Southern Ocean, reanalysis products show no significant shift in the annual mean latitude of zonal wind jets between 1979–
L1423@P17: 2009 (Swart et al., 2015a). Similarly, a variety of methods applied to satellite data have found no long-term trend and no statistically
L1424@P17: significant correlation of ACC position with winds (Gille, 2014; Chapman, 2017; Chambers, 2018). The discrepancy between these
L1425@P17: studies and those assessed in WGI AR5 appears to be caused by issues associated with using a fixed sea surface height contour as
L1426@P17: a proxy for frontal position in the presence of strongly eddying fields (Chapman, 2014) and large-scale increases in sea surface height
L1427@P17: consistent with mean global trends in sea level rise (Gille, 2014). The increase in sea surface height is ascribed largely to warming-driven
L1428@P17: steric expansion in the upper ocean, but the mechanism driving such warming is still uncertain (Gille, 2014). These recent findings do
L1429@P17: not preclude more local changes in frontal position, but it is now assessed as unlikely that there has been a statistically significant net
L1430@P17: southward movement of the mean ACC position over the past 20 years.
L1431@P17: Overturning Circulation and Water Mass Formation
L1432@P17: The Southern Ocean is the key region globally for the upwelling of interior ocean waters to the surface, enabling waters that were last
L1433@P17: ventilated in the pre-industrial era to interact with the industrial-era atmosphere and the cryosphere. New water masses are produced
L1434@P17: that sink back into the ocean interior. Such export of both extremely cold and dense Antarctic Bottom Water and the lighter mode and
L1435@P17: intermediate waters (Figure CB7.1) represents important pathways for surface properties to be sequestered from the atmosphere for
L1436@P17: decades to millennia. This upwelling and sinking constitutes a two-limbed overturning circulation, by which much of the global deep
L1437@P17: ocean is renewed.
L1438@P17: The Southern Ocean overturning circulation plays a strong role in mediating climate change via the transfer of heat and carbon
L1439@P17: (including that of anthropogenic origin) with the atmosphere (Sections  3.2.1.2;  5.2.2.2); it also has an impact on sea ice
L1440@P17-18: extent and concentration, with implications for climate via albedo (Section  3.2.1.1). It acts to oxygenate the ocean interior 221

L1443@P18: and  sequesters nutrients that ultimately end up supporting a  significant fraction of primary production in the rest of the world
L1444@P18: ocean (Section 5.2.2.2). The upwelling waters in the overturning bring heat to the Antarctic shelf seas, with consequences for ice
L1445@P18: shelves, marine-terminating glaciers and the stability of the Antarctic Ice Sheet (AIS) (Section 3.3.1). The lower limb of this overturning
L1446@P18: circulation supplies Antarctic Bottom Water that forms the abyssal layer of much of the world ocean (Section 3.2.1.2; 5.2.2.2).
L1447@P18: It is challenging to measure the Southern Ocean overturning directly, and misinterpretation of Waugh et al. (2013) led to AR5
L1448@P18: erroneously reporting the upper cell to have slowed (AR5 WGI, Section  3.6.4). However, additional indirect estimates since AR5
L1449@P18: provide support for the increase in the upper ocean overturning proposed by Waugh et al. (2013). Waugh (2014) and Ting and Holzer
L1450@P18: (2017) suggest that over the 1990s–2000s water mass ages changed in a manner consistent with an increase in upwelling and
L1451@P18: overturning. However, inverse analyses suggest that such overturning experiences significant inter-decadal variability in response

L1519@P19: Projections
L1520@P19: Projections of future trends in the Southern Ocean are dominated by the potential for a continued strengthening of the westerly winds
L1521@P19: (Bracegirdle et al., 2013), as well as a combination of warming and increased freshwater input from both increased net precipitation
L1522@P19: and changes in sea ice export (Downes and Hogg, 2013). Dynamical considerations and numerical simulations indicate that, if further
L1523@P19: increases in the westerly winds are sustained, then it is very likely that the eddy field will continue to grow in intensity (Morrison and
L1524@P19: Hogg, 2013; Munday et al., 2013), with potential consequences for the upper-ocean overturning circulation and transport of tracers
L1525@P19: (Abernathey and Ferreira, 2015) (including heat, carbon, oxygen and nutrients), and likely that the mean position and strength of the
L1526@P19: ACC will remain only weakly sensitive to winds.
L1527@P19: The considerable Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5  (CMIP5) inter-model variations in Southern Ocean time-mean
L1528@P19: circulation projections reported in WGI AR5 (Meijers et al., 2012; Downes and Hogg, 2013) remain largely unchanged. Some of the
L1529@P19: differences in projected changes have been found to be correlated with biases in the various models’ ability to simulate the historical
L1530@P19: state of the Southern Ocean, such as mixed layer depth (Sallée et al., 2013a) and westerly wind jet latitude (Bracegirdle et al., 2013).
L1531@P19: This suggests that bias reduction against observed historical metrics (Russell et al., 2018) in future generations of coupled models
L1532@P19: (e.g., Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6)) should lead to improved confidence in aspects of projected Southern
L1533@P19: Ocean changes. CMIP5 models suggest that the subduction of mode and intermediate water will increase (Sallée et al., 2013b), which
L1534@P19: will affect oxygen and nutrient transports, and the overall transport of the Southern Ocean upper overturning cell will increase by up
L1538@P19: processes in global models. Further uncertainty derives from increased meltwater from the AIS not being considered in the CMIP5
L1539@P19: climate models, despite its potential for significant impact on Southern Ocean dynamics and the global climate, and its potential for
L1540@P19: positive feedbacks (Bronselaer et al., 2018). Due to these uncertainties, low confidence is therefore ascribed to the CMIP5-based
L1541@P19: model projections of future Southern Ocean circulation and watermasses.

L2252@P27: 3.2.3.2 Southern Ocean
L2253@P27: Marine ecosystem dynamics in the Antarctic region are dominated by
L2254@P27: the ACC and its frontal systems (Cross-Chapter Box 7 in Chapter 3),
L2255@P27: subpolar gyres, polar seasonality, the annual advance and retreat of
L2256@P27: sea ice (Section  3.2.1.1) and the supply of limiting micronutrients
L2257@P27: for productivity (most commonly iron) (Section  5.2.2.5). Antarctic
L2258@P27: krill (Euphausia superba) play a  central role in Southern Ocean
L2273@P27: Sections  3.2.1,  3.2.2) will be important in determining future
L2274@P27: states of Southern Ocean ecosystems (Constable et al., 2014; Gutt
L2275@P27: et al., 2015) (medium confidence). However, there is a need to better
L2276@P27: characterise the nature and importance of indirect responses to
L2277@P27: physical change using models and observations. Important advances
L2278@P27: have also been made since AR5 in (i) identifying key variables to
L2279@P27: detect and attribute change in Southern Ocean ecosystems, as part
L2280@P27: of long-term circumpolar modelling designs (Constable et al., 2016),
L2281@P27: and (ii) refining methods for using sea ice projections from global
L2282@P27: climate models in ecological studies and ecosystem models for the
L2283@P27: Southern Ocean (Cavanagh et al., 2017).
L2284@P27: 3.2.3.2.1 Plankton and pelagic primary production
L2285@P27: Changes in column-integrated phytoplankton biomass for the
L2286@P27: Southern Ocean are coupled with changes in the spatial extent of
L2287@P27: ice-free waters, suggesting little overall change in biomass per area
L2288@P27: at the circumpolar scale (Behrenfeld et al., 2016). Arrigo et al. (2008)
L2289@P27: also report no overall trend in remotely-sensed column-integrated
L2290@P27: primary production south of 50ºS from 1998 to 2006. At a regional
L2291@P27: scale, local-scale forcings (e.g.,  retreating glaciers, topographically
L2292@P27: steered circulation and sea ice duration) and associated changes in
